prompt: When structuring a technical explainer like 'Kerberoasting for a Tier 1 reader,' what is the primary design move for bridging the audience gap?
choices: Build the new material explicitly on concepts the audience already has (e.g. offline hash cracking) before introducing new primitives like SPNs and TGS tickets
Use simpler vocabulary throughout even if it makes the explanation less precise
Include every known attack variant so the reader sees the full threat landscape
Skip the defense/mitigation section since a beginner can't implement it yet

prompt: Why does Kerberoasting let any authenticated domain user obtain crackable material for a service account, without needing elevated privileges first?
choices: Any domain user can request a TGS for any registered SPN, and that ticket is encrypted with a key derived from the service account's own password hash, which can be attacked offline
The attacker must already hold domain admin rights before requesting any service ticket
The KDC returns the service account's password in plaintext to any requester
The Key Distribution Center verifies the requester owns the SPN before issuing a ticket

prompt: A mentee's SQLi payload is theoretically correct but fails when typed into Juice Shop's login form, leading them to wrongly conclude the app isn't vulnerable. What is the most productive thing for a mentor to do, without handing over a payload?
choices: Ask them to check what happens to their input before it reaches the server, pointing them back toward the Burp Suite proxy skill they already have
Give them the exact working payload string so they can confirm the vulnerability exists
Tell them to abandon the challenge since the app has clearly been patched
Explain that client-side validation proves the server-side query is also safely parameterized

prompt: What is the correct shape of written feedback on a wrong-but-reasoned exploit attempt?
choices: Affirm the parts of their reasoning that were sound, name precisely where the model diverged from reality, point at a tool or concept to revisit, and require them to re-test it themselves
Quietly substitute the correct payload into their terminal so they see the working exploit
Tell them to keep trying random variations until something works
Give no technical detail at all so they are forced to start over from scratch

prompt: What hint-ladder design is recommended for a beginner-friendly CTF challenge?
choices: A tiered ladder (roughly three steps) that first names the category or tool, then narrows to the mechanism, then confirms the near-final step, each costing more points, without ever giving the literal payload or flag
One all-or-nothing hint that states the vulnerability class and the fix directly
No hints at all, so solvers either get it or don't
A full walkthrough available from the start of the event

prompt: Why should CTF or workshop material reference only retired or concluded competitions for structural inspiration, rather than a currently live one?
choices: Reusing or spoiling a still-open challenge undermines the competition for everyone still working it and breaks the no-spoiler norm the community relies on
Retired competitions have noticeably better server infrastructure
Current competitions legally forbid any write-ups under any circumstances
Retired challenges are always technically simpler to study

prompt: What practically distinguishes adapting the same technical content into a conference-style talk versus a blog post?
choices: A talk needs timed, slide-per-idea pacing and a pre-recorded demo fallback for when the live demo fails; a blog post can go deeper in linear prose and push edge cases into links or footnotes

A conference talk never needs an introductory hook or framing

prompt: In a self-hosted CTFd beginner workshop, why choose dynamic (decay) scoring over flat per-challenge points?
choices: It lowers a challenge's point value as more teams solve it, which keeps the event from being decided purely by who is fastest on the easy challenges and keeps later solvers motivated
It automatically disables all hints once enabled
It hides the leaderboard from all participants for the entire event
CTFd requires decay scoring and offers no alternative scoring mode
